findings.body:
Removing `os.path.basename` and joining `request.args.get("path", name)` into `REPORTS` lets a client read any file the process can open. `GET /reports/x?path=../../etc/passwd` resolves to `/srv/reports/../../etc/passwd`; `GET /reports/x?path=/etc/passwd` makes `os.path.join` discard `REPORTS` and serve `/etc/passwd`. Flask `send_file` does not confine the path.

Serve nested reports with `send_from_directory(REPORTS, relative)` (or `safe_join` plus an abspath-prefix check) so the resolved path must stay under `/srv/reports`.

summary:
This change removes the only path sanitizer (`os.path.basename`) and joins an unsanitized query parameter into `send_file`. That is a path-traversal / arbitrary-file-read on a public download route.

`GET /reports/x?path=../../etc/passwd` becomes `/srv/reports/../../etc/passwd`. `GET /reports/x?path=/etc/passwd` makes `os.path.join` drop `REPORTS` and open `/etc/passwd` directly. Flask's `send_file` does not confine the path to a directory.

Nested folders such as `2024/q3` can be served safely with `send_from_directory(REPORTS, relative)` (or `werkzeug.security.safe_join` plus an abspath-prefix check). Do not merge until that confinement is in place.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch replaces basename-sanitized `name` with unsanitized `request.args.get("path", name)` joined into REPORTS and passed to send_file, so `?path=../../etc/passwd` or `?path=/etc/passwd` can read arbitrary files. That is a real critical arbitrary-file-read regression.
